In 1996, a WHO study reported that the strength of the observed relationship for cervical adenocarcinomas and adenosquamous carcinomas and oral contraceptives was about the same as that for invasive squamous cell cervical carcinomas.7 Human papillomavirus (HPV) has a role in the aetiology of cer- vical cancer; women who are HPV positive and using oral con- traceptives may be at increased risk of cervical neoplasm.8,9 A pooled analysis of 8 case-control studies in women who tested positive for HPV DNA suggested risk of invasive squamous cer- vical cancer or carcinoma in situ was increased about threefold in those who used oral contraceptives for 5 years or more.10 Data on the risk of cervical cancer with progestogen-only con- traceptives are limited. WHO have investigated any possible link between the use of medroxyprogesterone acetate as a long- acting injectable contraceptive and cervical neoplasia. Analysis showed a small non-significant elevated risk (1.11; 95% confi- dence interval 0.9 to 1.29), and no clear association with duration of use.11 A later case-control study12 found no significant associ- ation between injectable progestogen contraceptives and inva- sive cervical cancer risk. 1.
